questions.question: What is a Promise and how do its states work?
questions.title: Promises Basics
questions.direct_answer: A Promise is an object representing a value that will be available later (or an eventual failure). It has three states: pending (initial), fulfilled (resolved with a value), rejected (failed with a reason). Once settled (fulfilled or rejected), it's immutable — a promise settles exactly once. .then attaches fulfillment handlers, .catch rejection handlers, .finally cleanup; each returns a new promise, enabling chains.

sections.title: Interview Answer
Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> pending
    pending --> fulfilled: resolve(value)
    pending --> rejected: reject(reason)
    fulfilled --> [*]: .then handlers fire
    rejected --> [*]: .catch handlers fire
    note right of fulfilled: settled = permanent\nno re-settle
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
Why promises replaced callbacks (the design problem they solve): nested callbacks ('callback hell') had inversion of control — you hand your continuation to an API and hope it calls it once, with the right args. Promises return that control: you attach handlers to an object YOU hold, and the guarantee (settles once, in order, never sync-blocked) is enforced by the platform.

The microtask guarantee (the depth marker): .then callbacks run as microtasks — after the current synchronous code, before the next macrotask (verified: a .then logged before a setTimeout(0)). This ordering is spec-mandated, not scheduling luck. The consequence: promise chains always observe state consistently within a tick, which is what makes async/await's sequential illusion work.

The combinator family (the follow-up): Promise.all (fail-fast parallelism — all fulfill or the first rejection wins, and the others' results are DISCARDED even though they continue), allSettled (partial failure tolerated — you inspect each {status, value/reason}), race (first to settle, fulfillment or rejection), any (first FULFILLMENT; rejections ignored unless all fail, then AggregateError). Choosing between them is a real interview question: all for must-have-all data, allSettled for best-effort batches (upload with per-file retries), race for timeouts, any for redundant sources (fastest mirror).
